title: Ceva's Theorem: Non-Euclidean Extensions via Unified Ratio Framework
description: Extends Ceva's theorem to spherical and hyperbolic geometry using an abstract generalized framework. All three versions — trigonometric (Euclidean), spherical, and hyperbolic — reduce to the same algebraic identity: a product of three ratios ρ(a)/ρ(b) equals 1, where ρ is the identity (Euclidean), sin (spherical), or sinh (hyperbolic). The formalization includes flat-limit theorems proving that both sin(x)/x → 1 and sinh(x)/x → 1 as x → 0, formally connecting the non-Euclidean versions to the Euclidean case for small triangles.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: GeneralizedCevianConfig structure unifying Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic configurations
generalized_ceva: abstract algebraic core shared by all three geometry types
ceva_unified_principle: parametric version with arbitrary ratio function ρ
sinh_pos_of_pos: sinh is positive for positive arguments, proved from exp monotonicity
hasDerivAt_sinh: derivative of sinh proved from the definition sinh = (exp(x) - exp(-x))/2
spherical_flat_limit and hyperbolic_flat_limit: sin(x)/x → 1 and sinh(x)/x → 1 as x → 0
Formal proofs of spherical_ceva and hyperbolic_ceva from the unified principle
Medians concurrent lemmas for both spherical and hyperbolic geometry

overview.historicalContext: Giovanni Ceva published his concurrency theorem in De lineis rectis (1678), unaware that Yūsuf al-Muʾtaman ibn Hūd had proved it in 11th-century Andalusia (Kitāb al-Istikmāl). The trigonometric form — using sines of split angles rather than segment ratios — was known to 18th-century geometers and appears in works on spherical trigonometry used for celestial navigation and geodesy. Non-Euclidean geometry, discovered independently by Bolyai and Lobachevsky around 1830, revealed that hyperbolic and spherical Ceva conditions take the same algebraic form with sin or sinh replacing linear distances. Lobachevsky himself noted the hyperbolic analogue in his foundational papers. In the 20th century, Athanase Papadopoulos systematically studied hyperbolic analogues of classical Euclidean theorems (including Menelaus, Ceva, and Stewart) as part of a broader program connecting spherical and hyperbolic geometry through the theory of metric spaces of curvature ≤ κ. The key insight — that all three Ceva conditions are instances of a single algebraic identity parameterized by a 'ratio function' ρ (id, sin, or sinh) — reflects the Riemannian geometry principle that local geometry is Euclidean, and non-Euclidean effects are encoded by replacing linear measures with trigonometric ones.
overview.problemStatement: Do analogues of Ceva's theorem hold in spherical and hyperbolic geometry? The answer is yes: in spherical geometry, cevians of a geodesic triangle are concurrent iff sin(BD)·sin(CE)·sin(AF) = sin(DC)·sin(EA)·sin(FB) for arc-length segments; in hyperbolic geometry, the condition is sinh(BD)·sinh(CE)·sinh(AF) = sinh(DC)·sinh(EA)·sinh(FB) for hyperbolic distances. Both reduce to the same algebraic identity as the Euclidean case.
overview.proofStrategy: The algebraic core of Ceva's theorem is: given six positive reals a, b, c, d, e, f, the product (a/b)(c/d)(e/f) = 1 iff ace = bdf. This is purely division algebra and requires only positivity of the denominators. For each geometry, the relevant quantities (sin of arc lengths for spherical, sinh of hyperbolic distances) are positive in the appropriate domain. The positivity of sin on (0,π) is from Mathlib; the positivity of sinh on (0,∞) is proved from the strict monotonicity of exp. The flat limits are derived from HasDerivAt at zero.
keyInsights: All three Ceva conditions are instances of a single algebraic identity: ρ(a)/ρ(b) · ρ(c)/ρ(d) · ρ(e)/ρ(f) = 1 ↔ ρ(a)ρ(c)ρ(e) = ρ(b)ρ(d)ρ(f), where ρ is id (Euclidean), sin (spherical), or sinh (hyperbolic).

The GeneralizedCevianConfig structure encodes validity conditions—six positivity proofs—directly as structure fields, so the type system guarantees well-formedness and the algebraic proof need only invoke positivity once.
sinh_pos_of_pos is derived from first principles using exp strict monotonicity: exp(x) > 1 > exp(-x) for x > 0 implies sinh(x) = (exp(x) - exp(-x))/2 > 0 by linarith.

hasDerivAt_sinh is proved by composing the chain rule on exp(-x) via hasDerivAt_neg, then algebraically simplifying (exp(x) - (-1)·exp(-x))/2 = (exp(x) + exp(-x))/2 = cosh(x) via ring—a calculation that also verifies the standard formula sinh'(x) = cosh(x).
The flat limit theorems (sin(t)/t → 1, sinh(t)/t → 1 as t → 0) follow from HasDerivAt.tendsto_slope_zero, converting the derivative at 0 directly to the difference quotient limit without L'Hôpital.

The domain constraint difference is geometrically meaningful: spherical arc lengths are in (0, π) because a side of a non-degenerate geodesic triangle on a hemisphere cannot equal or exceed π, while hyperbolic distances are unbounded—requiring only positivity in HyperbolicCevianConfig.
prerequisites: Euclidean Ceva's theorem and its algebraic proof
Spherical trigonometry: geodesics, arc lengths, sine rule on spheres
Hyperbolic geometry: Poincaré disk model, hyperbolic distance, hyperbolic sine
Differential calculus: derivatives of sin and sinh at zero
Basic Mathlib measure theory and filter convergence

conclusion.summary: The non-Euclidean extensions of Ceva's theorem are formally verified with 18 theorems and 0 sorries. The abstract framework (GeneralizedCevianConfig, ceva_unified_principle) cleanly separates the geometry from the algebra, making the proof structure transparent. The flat-limit theorems provide a rigorous formal connection between the three geometric settings.
conclusion.implications: The unified approach suggests a general pattern for non-Euclidean geometry: classical theorems involving ratios of lengths often have non-Euclidean versions obtained by replacing lengths with sin (spherical) or sinh (hyperbolic). This pattern appears in the law of sines, Menelaus' theorem, and trigonometric identities. The sinh derivative proof (hasDerivAt_sinh) is a useful standalone result not easily found in Mathlib.
openQuestions: Can the unified Ceva framework be extended to arbitrary curvature κ using the functions sin_κ (Jacobi sine for curvature κ)?
What is the hyperbolic analogue of Menelaus' theorem in this framework?
Can the abstract GeneralizedCevianConfig be used to prove non-Euclidean versions of other concurrence theorems (e.g., hyperbolic angle bisectors)?
Does the flat limit argument extend to a formal proof that the hyperbolic and spherical Ceva conditions converge to the Euclidean one for triangles on a manifold of shrinking curvature?

sections.title: Imports and Module Documentation
sections.summary: Mathlib imports for real analysis, trigonometry, and derivatives, plus a comprehensive module docstring listing the three Ceva variants (trigonometric, spherical, hyperbolic) and the unified algebraic approach.

sections.title: Part 1: Generalized Ceva Framework
sections.summary: Defines GeneralizedCevianConfig (six positive reals representing geometric measures), generalizedCevaProduct, and the algebraic core theorem: the product of three ratios equals 1 iff the numerator product equals the denominator product.

sections.title: Part 2: Trigonometric Ceva (Euclidean)
sections.summary: Defines TrigCevianConfig (six split angles at triangle vertices, bounded in (0,π)), converts to generalized form using Mathlib's sin_pos_of_pos_of_lt_pi, and proves the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem.

sections.title: Part 3: Spherical Ceva's Theorem
sections.summary: Defines SphericalCevianConfig (geodesic arc lengths in (0,π)), converts to generalized form via sin positivity, and proves that geodesic cevians on a sphere are concurrent iff the sine product condition holds.

sections.title: Part 4: Hyperbolic Ceva's Theorem
sections.summary: Proves sinh_pos_of_pos (key positivity helper derived from exp monotonicity), defines HyperbolicCevianConfig (hyperbolic distances, positivity only), and proves the hyperbolic cevian concurrency condition via sinh product.

sections.title: Part 5: Unified Theory — Curvature Parameter
sections.summary: States ceva_unified_principle with a generic higher-order ratio function ρ, then derives the Euclidean (ρ=id), spherical (ρ=sin), and hyperbolic (ρ=sinh) specializations as one-line corollaries.

sections.title: Part 6: Special Cases — Medians
sections.summary: Verifies spherical and hyperbolic medians (geodesic bisectors) are concurrent: equal measures trivially satisfy the Ceva product-equals-one condition via div_self.

sections.title: Part 7: Flat Limits — Connecting the Three Geometries
sections.summary: Proves spherical_flat_limit (sin(t)/t → 1), derives HasDerivAt for sinh from exp chain rule, proves hyperbolic_flat_limit (sinh(t)/t → 1), and bundles both as flat_limit_connects_geometries, formally showing all three Ceva conditions coincide for infinitesimally small triangles.

mainTheorems.name: ceva_unified_principle
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < ρ bd → … → 0 < ρ fb → (ρ bd / ρ dc * (ρ ce / ρ ea) * (ρ af / ρ fb) = 1 ↔ ρ bd * ρ ce * ρ af = ρ dc * ρ ea * ρ fb)
mainTheorems.significance: The organising theorem: for ANY positive 'measure' ρ, the cevian product-of-ratios equals 1 iff the cross-products of measures agree. Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic Ceva are all this one statement with ρ = id, sin, sinh — a single algebraic identity underlying concurrency across all three geometries.
mainTheorems.description: Clears denominators via div_mul_div_comm twice and div_eq_one_iff_eq, using positivity of the ρ-values to justify the nonzero divisors.

mainTheorems.name: generalized_ceva
mainTheorems.statement: generalizedCevaProduct cfg = 1 ↔ cfg.bd * cfg.ce * cfg.af = cfg.dc * cfg.ea * cfg.fb
mainTheorems.significance: Abstract form on a GeneralizedCevianConfig (six positive measures bundled with their positivity proofs). The structure-packaged version of the unified principle that the three geometry-specific theorems reduce to.
mainTheorems.description: Same denominator-clearing argument as ceva_unified_principle, drawing the nonzero hypotheses from the config's *_pos fields.

mainTheorems.name: trigonometric_ceva
mainTheorems.statement: trigCevaProduct cfg = 1 ↔ sin ∠BAD * sin ∠CBE * sin ∠ACF = sin ∠DAC * sin ∠EBA * sin ∠FCA
mainTheorems.significance: Trigonometric Ceva (Euclidean): cevians AD, BE, CF concur iff the sine-ratio product is 1. More fundamental than the length-ratio form precisely because it transfers verbatim to non-Euclidean geometries.
mainTheorems.description: Rewrites through trigCevaProduct_eq_generalized and applies generalized_ceva to the sin-valued config.

mainTheorems.name: spherical_ceva
mainTheorems.statement: sphericalCevaProduct cfg = 1 ↔ sin(arc BD) * sin(arc CE) * sin(arc AF) = sin(arc DC) * sin(arc EA) * sin(arc FB)
mainTheorems.significance: Spherical Ceva: on the sphere, arc-length ratios are replaced by their sines, and concurrency holds iff the sine cross-products agree. The spherical instance of the unified principle (ρ = sin on arcs in (0,π)).

mainTheorems.name: hyperbolic_ceva
mainTheorems.statement: hyperbolicCevaProduct cfg = 1 ↔ sinh(BD) * sinh(CE) * sinh(AF) = sinh(DC) * sinh(EA) * sinh(FB)
mainTheorems.significance: Hyperbolic Ceva: in the hyperbolic plane, sinh of the side-distances replaces the Euclidean ratios; concurrency holds iff the sinh cross-products agree. The hyperbolic instance of the unified principle (ρ = sinh).

mainTheorems.name: ceva_euclidean_specialization
mainTheorems.statement: bd / dc * (ce / ea) * (af / fb) = 1 ↔ bd * ce * af = dc * ea * fb
mainTheorems.significance: The classical Euclidean Ceva recovered as ρ = id in the unified principle. Makes explicit that the ordinary length-ratio theorem is one specialization among three.
mainTheorems.description: ceva_unified_principle applied to id with the six positivity hypotheses.

mainTheorems.name: ceva_spherical_specialization
mainTheorems.statement: sin bd / sin dc * (sin ce / sin ea) * (sin af / sin fb) = 1 ↔ sin bd * sin ce * sin af = sin dc * sin ea * sin fb
mainTheorems.significance: Spherical Ceva as the ρ = sin specialization of the unified principle, with arcs constrained to (0,π) so every sine is positive.
mainTheorems.description: ceva_unified_principle with ρ = Real.sin, discharging positivity by Real.sin_pos_of_pos_of_lt_pi on each arc.

mainTheorems.name: ceva_hyperbolic_specialization
mainTheorems.statement: sinh bd / sinh dc * (sinh ce / sinh ea) * (sinh af / sinh fb) = 1 ↔ sinh bd * sinh ce * sinh af = sinh dc * sinh ea * sinh fb
mainTheorems.significance: Hyperbolic Ceva as the ρ = sinh specialization of the unified principle, for positive distances.
mainTheorems.description: ceva_unified_principle with ρ = Real.sinh, discharging positivity by sinh_pos_of_pos.

mainTheorems.name: flat_limit_connects_geometries
mainTheorems.statement: Tendsto (fun t => t⁻¹ * sin t) (𝓝[≠] 0) (𝓝 1) ∧ Tendsto (fun t => t⁻¹ * sinh t) (𝓝[≠] 0) (𝓝 1)
mainTheorems.significance: The unifying limit: as scale → 0 both sin t / t and sinh t / t tend to 1, so the spherical and hyperbolic Ceva conditions degenerate to the Euclidean one. Formalises how curved-space concurrency reduces to the flat case in the small-triangle limit.

mainTheorems.name: spherical_flat_limit
mainTheorems.statement: Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => t⁻¹ * Real.sin t) (nhdsWithin 0 {0}ᶜ) (nhds 1)
mainTheorems.significance: sin t / t → 1 as t → 0: the spherical measure sin(arc) becomes the flat arc length in the small-scale limit. One half of the flat-limit bridge.
mainTheorems.description: The difference-quotient of sin at 0 is its derivative cos 0 = 1 (Real.hasDerivAt_sin 0 |>.tendsto_slope_zero).

mainTheorems.name: hyperbolic_flat_limit
mainTheorems.statement: Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => t⁻¹ * Real.sinh t) (nhdsWithin 0 {0}ᶜ) (nhds 1)
mainTheorems.significance: sinh t / t → 1 as t → 0: the hyperbolic measure sinh(dist) becomes the flat distance in the small-scale limit. The other half of the flat-limit bridge.
mainTheorems.description: The difference-quotient of sinh at 0 is its derivative cosh 0 = 1, using hasDerivAt_sinh 0.

mainTheorems.name: hasDerivAt_sinh
mainTheorems.significance: The derivative of sinh is cosh, supplied here because it drives the hyperbolic flat-limit. A small piece of analytic infrastructure the file needs beyond Mathlib's sin support.
mainTheorems.description: Differentiates sinh = (exp x - exp (-x))/2 via hasDerivAt_exp and the chain rule on exp(-x).

mainTheorems.name: sinh_pos_of_pos
mainTheorems.significance: Positivity of sinh on the positive reals — the hyperbolic analogue of sin-positivity, ensuring the hyperbolic Ceva measures are valid (nonzero) divisors.
mainTheorems.description: From sinh x = (exp x - exp (-x))/2 with exp x > exp 0 = 1 > exp(-x).

mainTheorems.name: spherical_medians_concurrent
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < a → a < Real.pi → sin a / sin a * (sin a / sin a) * (sin a / sin a) = 1
mainTheorems.significance: Corollary: spherical medians concur. When D, E, F are midpoints (equal arcs on each side), the spherical Ceva product is trivially 1 — the sphere's version of the centroid.
mainTheorems.description: div_self on the nonzero sin a (positive on (0,π)).

mainTheorems.name: hyperbolic_medians_concurrent
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < d → sinh d / sinh d * (sinh d / sinh d) * (sinh d / sinh d) = 1
mainTheorems.significance: Corollary: hyperbolic medians concur. Equal side-distances make the hyperbolic Ceva product 1 — the hyperbolic centroid.
mainTheorems.description: div_self on the nonzero sinh d (positive for d > 0).

mainTheorems.name: trigCevaProduct_eq_generalized
mainTheorems.significance: Bridge lemma: the trigonometric Ceva product is definitionally the generalized product on the sin-valued config. Lets trigonometric_ceva inherit generalized_ceva.
mainTheorems.description: rfl after unfolding the two products and the toGeneralized coercion.

mainTheorems.name: sphericalCevaProduct_eq_generalized
mainTheorems.significance: Bridge lemma routing spherical Ceva to the abstract form.

mainTheorems.name: hyperbolicCevaProduct_eq_generalized
mainTheorems.significance: Bridge lemma routing hyperbolic Ceva to the abstract form.
